Founded on 24 October 1946, FK Sarajevo was the most successful club from [[SR Bosnia and Herzegovina]] in [[SFR Yugoslavia|Yugoslavia]], winning two [[Yugoslav First League]] titles, finishing runners-up on two other occasions, reaching the [[Yugoslav Cup]] final twice and placing 6th in the Yugoslav First League [[Yugoslav First League#All-Time First Yugoslav League Table|all-time table]].{{cite web|url=http://strategija.org/vecna-lista-fudbalskih-prvenstava-sfr-jugoslavije/|title=Večna lista fudbalskih prvenstava SFR Jugoslavije|date=3 February 2013 |publisher=Strategija.org|access-date=17 March 2014|archive-date=23 February 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140223111317/http://strategija.org/vecna-lista-fudbalskih-prvenstava-sfr-jugoslavije/|url-status=live}} Today, FK Sarajevo is one of the most prominent members of the [[Premier League of Bosnia and Herzegovina]], where it has won five [[Premier League of Bosnia and Herzegovina|Bosnian championships]], eight [[Bosnia and Herzegovina Football Cup|Bosnian Cups]] and one [[Bosnian Supercup]]. Furthermore, the club finished runners-up in the national championship another seven times. It is ranked second in the Premier League of Bosnia and Herzegovina all-time table. FK Sarajevo is the most popular football club in the country, alongside [[FK Željezničar Sarajevo|FK Željezničar]], with whom it shares a fierce rivalry in the [[Sarajevo derby]], often called the ''Eternal derby'' ([[Bosnian language|Bosnian]]: Vječiti derbi).{{cite web |title=Sarajevo stage set for unique eternal derby |url=https://www.uefa.com/news-media/news/0203-0f8821514c79-9b933c0b69c1-1000--sarajevo-stage-set-for-unique-eternal-derby/ |website=UEFA.com |date=2 November 2012 |access-date=15 June 2025}} This fixture is not only Bosnia and Herzegovina's premier football rivalry, but it has also been recognized internationally, being featured among [[FourFourTwo]]’s ''50 Biggest Derbies in the World''.{{cite web |title=FourFourTwo's 50 Biggest Derbies in the World |url=https://www.fourfourtwo.com/features/fourfourtwos-50-biggest-derbies-world |website=FourFourTwo |date= 25 April 2016|access-date=15 June 2025}} The club plays its home matches at the [[Asim Ferhatović Hase Stadium]], also known as the Koševo Stadium, named after legendary club striker [[Asim Ferhatović]], and located in the city's [[Koševo]] neighborhood. The stadium has a current capacity of 34,700 and is the largest in the country.{{cite web|url=http://www.worldstadiums.com/europe/countries/bosnia_herzegovina.shtml|title=World Stadiums – Stadiums in Bosnia & Herzegovina|work=worldstadiums.com|access-date=27 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170501131039/http://www.worldstadiums.com/europe/countries/bosnia_herzegovina.shtml|archive-date=1 May 2017|url-status=dead}} FK Sarajevo also operates the [[Butmir Training Centre]] in the [[Ilidža]] municipality, a state-of-the-art facility spanning 70,000 m² and opened in 2015. The centre includes multiple FIFA-standard pitches, modern fitness and rehabilitation infrastructure, and serves as the training base for the men’s, women’s, youth teams and [[FK Sarajevo B|Sarajevo B]].{{cite web|url=https://fksarajevo.ba/bs/novost/akademija-fk-sarajevo-razvija-vrhunske-sportske-talente-u-trening-centru-butmir/7607|title=Akademija FK Sarajevo razvija vrhunske sportske talente u Trening centru Butmir|date=15 May 2023|access-date=15 June 2025|language=bs|author=|publisher=fksarajevo.ba}}{{cite web|url=https://www.klix.ba/sport/nogomet/mirvic-se-pohvalio-zavrsenim-prvim-dijelom-radova-u-butmiru/240229084|title=Mirvić se pohvalio završenim prvim dijelom radova u Butmiru|date=29 February 2024|access-date=15 June 2025|language=bs|author=|publisher=Klix.ba}} The traditional colours of the club are [[maroon]] and white, with the home kit traditionally consisting of a maroon shirt, white shorts, and maroon socks - a combination that has become one of the most iconic and recognizable in Yugoslav and Bosnian sports.{{cite web|url=https://fk-sarajevo.ba/bs/klub/grb-i-boje/2|title=Grb i boje|date=15 June 2025|access-date=15 June 2025|language=bs|author=|publisher=fk-sarajevo.ba}} The club’s historic nickname is the Maroon-Whites ([[Bosnian language|Bosnian]]: Bordo-bijeli), in reference to its traditional maroon and white colours. Over the decades, the club has also been affectionately known as the Sarajevan Aghas ([[Bosnian language|Bosnian]]: Age Sarajlije), a nickname that alludes both to the [[Ottoman Bosnia and Herzegovina|Ottoman-era]] [[aghas]] and to a well-known [[sevdalinka]], "[[Vino piju nane age Sarajlije]]", which nostalgically evokes the city’s cultural identity. In recent years, another popular nickname has emerged: The Giants ([[Bosnian language|Bosnian]]: Divovi), inspired by [[Benjamin Isović]]’s football ballad, "[[Mi smo divovi]]" ([[English language|English]]: We Are Giants), which subsequently became the club’s official anthem.{{cite web|url=https://radiosarajevo.ba/sport/nogomet/benjamin-isovic-mi-smo-divovi-je-vise-od-navijacke-pjesme/237382|title=Benjamin Isović: 'Mi smo divovi' je više od navijačke pjesme|date=28 April 2016|access-date=15 June 2025|language=bs|author=|publisher=radiosarajevo.ba}} In addition to its domestic achievements, FK Sarajevo is widely regarded as the most significant exporter of footballing |website=Jabuka.tv |date=6 February 2024 |access-date=13 June 2025}} The club holds seven out of the ten highest player transfer fees in the history of Bosnian football, underlining its role as an |access-date=13 June 2025}} The club’s success in the transfer market is largely attributed to its renowned [[FK Sarajevo Youth School|youth academy]], which has consistently produced top-tier talent |access-date=13 June 2025}} Beyond its sporting achievements, FK Sarajevo holds a significant role in the social and cultural landscape of the capital. The club reflects Sarajevo’s [[multicultural]] character and has a broad support base representing diverse communities within the city, country and the wider region.{{cite web |title=FK Sarajevo: A Symbol of Sarajevo's Multicultural Identity |url=https://www.footballhistory.org/club/sarajevo.html |website=FootballHistory.org |access-date=15 June 2025}}{{cite web |title=From the war to Vincent Tan: the history that shaped FK Sarajevo |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2019/jul/09/fk-sarajevo-champions-league-qualifier-war-vincent-tan |website=The Guardian |date=9 July 2019 |access-date=15 June 2025}}{{cite web |title=Celtic come from behind to beat Sarajevo in first leg of Champions League qualifier |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/football/2019/07/09/celtic-come-behind-beat-saravejo-first-leg-champions-league/ |website=The Telegraph |date=9 July 2019 |access-date=15 June 2025}} ==History== {{Main|History of FK Sarajevo}} {{Further|topic=league performance|List of FK Sarajevo seasons}} FK Sarajevo was the only major [[Football team|football club]] founded by the post-[[World War II|war]] Yugoslav authorities in the city of Sarajevo. The club entered the Yugoslav First League in the [[1948–49 Yugoslav First League|1948–49]] season, and eventually competed in all but two seasons in the top tier. After [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]] gained independence from [[Yugoslavia]], FK Sarajevo became one of the country's biggest ambassadors, departing on a large world tour during the [[Bosnian War]] with the goal of gaining international support for the country's cause.{{cite web|url=http://www.oslobodjenje.ba/vijesti/5-april-1992-5-april-2012/utakmice-sirom-svijeta-prijem-u-vatikanu|title=Utakmice širom svijeta, prijem u Vatikanu|publisher=Oslobođenje.ba|language=bs|access-date=12 August 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150227211642/http://www.oslobodjenje.ba/vijesti/5-april-1992-5-april-2012/utakmice-sirom-svijeta-prijem-u-vatikanu|archive-date=27 February 2015}} ===Origins=== [[File:Sweden and Yugoslavia in Football final at the Olympic Games, London, 1948.jpg|thumb|left|upright|[[Miroslav Brozović]] (center), pictured representing [[Yugoslavia]] at the [[1948 Summer Olympics]], was named player-coach of Sarajevo in September of the same year]] FK Sarajevo was established on 24 October 1946, at a meeting held in the main hall of the [[FIS building]], as the result of a merger between local Sarajevo football clubs ''Udarnik'' (Vanguard) and ''Sloboda'' (Liberty).{{cite web|url=http://scsport.ba/vijesti/fk-sarajevo-slavi-68-rodjendan-titula-prvaka-najveca-zelja-navijaca/81902|title=FK Sarajevo slavi 68. rođendan|publisher=Scsport.ba|access-date=20 August 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141024140119/http://scsport.ba/vijesti/fk-sarajevo-slavi-68-rodjendan-titula-prvaka-najveca-zelja-navijaca/81902|archive-date=24 October 2014}} The club first appeared on the Yugoslav sports scene in 1946 under the name '''Fiskulturno društvo Torpedo''' ([[English language|English]]: Gymnastics Society Torpedo), a homage to [[Torpedo Moscow]]. The first chairman of the newly founded club was [[Safet Džinović]], while the positions of vice-chairmen were granted to Vojo Marković and Alojz Stanarević respectively. Furthermore, [[Josip Bulat (born 1905)|Josip Bulat]] was named manager.{{cite web|url=http://fksinfo.com/novosti/kako-je-nastao-torpedo/2585|title=Kako je nastao FK Sarajevo|publisher=Fksinfo.com|access-date=27 October 2014|archive-date=29 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141029012709/http://fksinfo.com/novosti/kako-je-nastao-torpedo/2585|url-status=live}} [[File:FK Sarajevo foundation plaque.jpg|thumb|A commemorative plaque on the [[FIS building]] in [[Centar, Sarajevo|central Sarajevo]] signifies the site where the club was established]] On 5 October 1947, on the proposal of then-editor-in-chief of the popular daily newspaper ''[[Oslobođenje]]'', Mirko Ostojić, the club name was changed to '''Fiskulturno društvo Sarajevo''' ([[English language|English]]: Gymnastics Society Sarajevo),{{cite web |title=Lična karta |url=https://fksarajevo.ba/klub/licna-karta|website=fksarajevo.ba |access-date=8 July 2023 |language=bs}} before being changed yet again to '''Sportsko društvo metalaca Sarajevo''' ([[English language|English]]: Sports Society of Metalworkers Sarajevo) a year later. Finally, on 20 May 1949 the name '''Fudbalski klub Sarajevo''' was adopted. The newly formed team, which inherited the results and league standings of Udarnik, was joined by selected players from both Udarnik and Sloboda. Namely, Hodžić, Vlajičić, Šarenkapa, Pauković, Fizović, Konjević, Radović, Viđen and Mustagrudić from the former, and [[Lev Mantula|Mantula]], [[Ivica Glavočević|Glavočević]], Tošić, Pecelj, [[Nerćes Novo|Novo]], Strinić, [[Đuka Lovrić|Đ. Lovrić]] and [[Safet Alajbegović|Alajbegović]] from the latter. The team played its first match on 3 November 1946. In September 1948 SDM Sarajevo was joined by Yugoslav footballing legend [[Miroslav Brozović]], who brought in a largely needed level of experience to the new team. The [[Mostar]] native previously wore the black and white jersey of [[FK Partizan]], as well as captaining the [[Yugoslavia national football team|Yugoslavia national team]]. Brozović was offered the position of player-manager which he accepted, turning his attention to promoting the team to the [[Yugoslav First League]].{{cite web|url=http://www.radiosarajevo.ba/novost/62616/junaci-bez-ulica-miroslav-meho-brozovic|title=Junaci bez ulica: Miroslav Meho Brozović|publisher=Radiosarajevo.ba|access-date=27 October 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140826210351/http://www.radiosarajevo.ba/novost/62616/junaci-bez-ulica-miroslav-meho-brozovic|archive-date=26 August 2014}} FK Sarajevo first entered the top-flight Yugoslav First League after eliminating [[Belgrade]] club Sloga. They drew the first match 3:3 in [[Novi Sad]], but then won the second match 5:1 in Sarajevo. The team was relegated after its first season in the First League but was promoted back to the top tier in 1950. From then on FK Sarajevo played in every season of the First League apart from 1957-58. The club's first taste of European competitions began during the 1960s when it took part in the [[1960 Mitropa Cup]]{{cite book|last=Pivoda|first=Aleš|title=Legenda se vrátila|language=cs|year=2013|page=35|isbn=978-80-86783-65-9}} and the [[1961–63 Balkans Cup]],{{cite web|title=2nd Balkan Cup 1961/63|url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesb/balkanclub63.html|publisher=[[Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation]]|first=George J.|last=Vassalos|date=14 March 2007|access-date=3 February 2023|archive-date=30 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221130132820/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesb/balkanclub63.html|url-status=live}} while the first continent-wide European competition the club took part in was the [[1962–63 Intertoto Cup]].{{cite web|url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesi/int62.html|title=Intertoto Cup 1962/63|publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation|access-date=20 August 2014|archive-date=13 July 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220713102157/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesi/int62.html|url-status=live}} ===Champions of Yugoslavia - Bosnian breakthrough=== Until FK Sarajevo's historic triumph, no club from any republic outside of SR Serbia and SR Croatia had ever claimed the Yugoslav First League title. The league had long been dominated by the so-called "Big Four" of Yugoslav football, but the Bosnian breakthrough finally arrived in the 1966–67 season, when FK Sarajevo emerged as champions. This victory not only marked a significant milestone for Bosnian football but also ended an unprecedented eight-season dominance by clubs from SR Serbia, who had held the national crown uninterrupted. ====The 1960s: First championship==== {{See also|1966–67 FK Sarajevo season|1966–67 Yugoslav First League}} [[File:Hajduk-Sarajevo Kup Maršala Tita 1966-1967.jpg|thumb|left| Stadion "[[Stadion Stari plac|Stari plac]]" in Split - host of the [[1966–67 Yugoslav Cup]] final between [[HNK Hajduk Split|Hajduk Split]] and Sarajevo]] {{Quote box|Friend, I can't play for money while being directed by others on how to play. I'm grateful they were fair and didn't make a fuss about it. I told them I could only play for Sarajevo.|[[Asim Ferhatović]], in an interview, after returning from a short stint with [[Fenerbahçe S.K. (football)|Fenerbahçe]]{{cite news| url=http://fksinfo.com/novosti/in-memoriam-asim-ferhatovic-19331987/1012| title=IN MEMORIAM: Asim Ferhatović (1933–1987)| language=bs| publisher=Fksinfo.ba| access-date=3 August 2016| archive-date=17 August 2016| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160817074742/http://fksinfo.com/novosti/in-memoriam-asim-ferhatovic-19331987/1012| url-status=live}}|align=right|width=350px}} A key player for Sarajevo in their early years was the legendary striker [[Asim Ferhatović]], known as Hase, who played for the club from 1952 to 1967. In the 1963–64 season, he was the top scorer in the First League with nineteen goals,{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joegtops.html |title=List of Topscorers Yugoslav First League 1963/64: Asim Ferhatović (19 goals) |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation |date=25 July 2014 |access-date=3 February 2023 |archive-date=9 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221209060010/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joegtops.html |url-status=live }} leading the club to a fourth-place finish. The following year, Sarajevo finished second to [[FK Partizan|Partizan Belgrade]].{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joegchamp.html |title=1966–67 FK Sarajevo: List of Champions |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation |date=25 July 2014 |access-date=3 February 2023 |archive-date=23 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230223153359/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joegchamp.html |url-status=live }} In the 1966–67 season, Sarajevo won their first [[Yugoslav First League]] title, becoming the first national champions from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The historic season began with Brozović as head coach, and the team had a strong start with consecutive wins against [[FK Sutjeska Nikšić|Sutjeska Nikšić]] and city rivals [[FK Željezničar|Željezničar]], followed by a draw against European Cup runners-up Partizan. Despite an early lead, Sarajevo managed seven points from their first three fixtures and, though not initially considered title favorites, they gained momentum with a victory against [[Hajduk Split]] on the Dalmatian coast. Four days later, Sarajevo defeated [[NK Olimpija Ljubljana (1945–2005)|Olimpija]] 2–1 at a sold-out Koševo Stadium. Hard-fought wins against [[HNK Rijeka|Rijeka]] and [[FK Crvena Zvezda|Red Star Belgrade]] followed, and by the winter break, Sarajevo had won 14 of their first 20 league matches, finishing the year in first place. The second part of the season opened with a 1–0 away win against [[Dinamo Zagreb]] in the last sixteen of the Yugoslav Cup, thanks to a stunning goal by [[Boško Antić]]. Although Sarajevo advanced past [[FK Napredak Kruševac|Napredak]] in the quarterfinals, they eventually lost in the Cup final to Hajduk Split at the [[Stadion Stari plac|Stari plac Stadium]] on May 24.{{cite news |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joegcupdetail.html |title=Cup of SFR Yugoslavia 1966/67 |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation |date=25 July 2014 |access-date=3 February 2023 |archive-date=9 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221209152002/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joegcupdetail.html |url-status=live }} The team quickly rebounded, defeating Red Star 3–1 at the [[Rajko Mitić Stadium]], with two goals from Antić and one from [[Boško Prodanović|Prodanović]]. A week later, they beat [[OFK Beograd]] by the same margin, but a surprising defeat to [[FK Vojvodina|Vojvodina]] in [[Novi Sad]] left them tied with Dinamo Zagreb with three games remaining. Sarajevo then defeated [[FK Vardar|Vardar]] with a [[Vahidin Musemić|Musemić]] brace, while Dinamo dropped points in Rijeka. In the final league match of the season, Sarajevo hosted [[NK Čelik Zenica|Čelik Zenica]] in front of 30,000 spectators and won 5–2, securing the club's first league title. =====European Cup last 16===== [[File:FK Sarajevo in Kuwait, 1969.jpg|thumb|upright|Sarajevo's tour of Kuwait in 1969 was one of many international tours the club undertook during the 1950s and 1960s, which included notable trips across Africa, the Middle East, and South America]] The league triumph qualified Sarajevo to the 1967–68 European Cup (today's UEFA Champions League), where they played their first tie against Cypriots [[Olympiakos Nicosia]], winning 5:3 on aggregate.{{cite news |url=http://uk.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/season=1967/matches/round=951/index.html |title=Sarajevo v Olympiakos Sept/Oct 1967 |publisher=UEFA |date=25 July 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921053328/http://uk.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/season%3D1967/matches/round%3D951/index.html |archive-date=21 September 2013 }} In the second round (one round short of the quarter-finals), Sarajevo was knocked out 2:1 on aggregate by eventual champions [[Manchester United]] of England, despite hosting a goalless draw in the first leg.{{cite news |url=http://uk.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/season=1967/matches/round=952/index.html |title=Sarajevo v Man. United Nov 1967 |publisher=UEFA |date=25 July 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921054034/http://uk.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/season%3D1967/matches/round%3D952/index.html |archive-date=21 September 2013 }} The first leg was played before an audience of 40,000 spectators and refereed by the Italian Francesco Francescon. The second leg played at [[Old Trafford]] ended in controversy after the ball went out of bounds prior to the hosts scoring their second goal. Notable Sarajevo players during this era included [[Boško Antić]], [[Mirsad Fazlagić]], [[Vahidin Musemić]], [[Fahrudin Prljača]] and [[Boško Prodanović]]. Shortly after winning its first Yugoslav league title FK Sarajevo endured a period of general stagnation.{{cite web|url=http://fksinfo.com/fk-sarajevo/historija|title=FK Sarajevo i period stagnacije|publisher=Fksinfo.com|language=bs|access-date=12 August 2014|archive-date=20 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140920221147/http://fksinfo.com/fk-sarajevo/historija|url-status=live}} The team entered the 1967/68 season as strong title favorites, but the campaign turned out to be a complete disaster. The maroon-whites, managed by former player [[Franjo Lovrić]], did not manage to enter the championship race in hopes of defending the title, finishing mere 7th.{{cite web|url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joeghist.html|title=Yugoslavia – List of Final Tables|publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation|access-date=12 August 2014|archive-date=9 July 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220709072232/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joeghist.html|url-status=live}} The club management quickly named [[Munib Saračević]] manager for the 1968/69 season, but this move also turned out to be fruitless. The team concluded the disappointing campaign 11th in the league standings. In the January 1971 transfer window, six members of the championship-winning generation, including Prodanović, Tešan, and Prljača, left the club. Three more players, including star player Boško Antić, departed in July of the same year. Despite a promising start to the next season, where the team led at the winter break, they only managed to finish 7th by the end of the season. The 1973–74 season saw the arrival of several new players, including future club legend [[Želimir Vidović]] and former Red Star Belgrade and [[Bayern Munich]] striker Dušan Jovanović. Additionally, 18-year-old [[Safet Sušić]] joined from [[NK Krivaja Zavidovići|Krivaja Zavidovići]] and would soon become a key player, driving the club to a second significant era of success in Yugoslav football.{{cite web|url=http://www.fksarajevo.ba/historija|title=FK Sarajevo 1970–1975|publisher=Fksarajevo.ba|language=bs|access-date=12 August 2014}}{{Dead link|date=March 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} In the first eleven seasons following their 1967 title win, FK Sarajevo's best achievements were a single 6th place league finish, two 7th place league finishes, and a quarter-final appearance in the Yugoslav Cup during the 1976–77 season. In the same year, the club narrowly avoided relegation, finishing just two points ahead of Napredak Kruševac. However, the 1978–79 season brought renewed hope for Sarajevo fans as the team finished 4th, behind Hajduk Split, Dinamo Zagreb, and Red Star Belgrade, signaling better times ahead. ====The 1980s: Second championship==== {{See also|1984–85 FK Sarajevo season|1984–85 Yugoslav First League}} {{football squad on pitch|align=left|GK=[[Miloš Đurković|Đurković]]|RB=[[Ferid Radeljaš|Radeljaš]]|RCB=[[Faruk Hadžibegić|Hadžibegić]]|LCB=[[Davor Jozić|Jozić]]|LB=[[Mirza Kapetanović|Kapetanović]]|RCM=[[Slaviša Vukićević|Vukićević]]|CM=[[Mehmed Janjoš|Janjoš]]|LCM=[[Senad Merdanović|Merdanović]]|CF=[[Husref Musemić|Musemić]]|caption=FK Sarajevo winning squad – 1984–85 Yugoslav First League champions|RSS=[[Dragan Jakovljević|Jakovljević]]|LSS=[[Predrag Pašić|Pašić]] [[Captain (association football)|(c)]]}} [[File:SusicPSG.jpg|thumb|[[Safet Sušić]] (centre) played for the club for nearly a decade before transferring to [[Paris Saint-Germain FC|Paris Saint-Germain]]. He later managed the [[Bosnia and Herzegovina national football team|Bosnia and Herzegovina]] at the [[2014 FIFA World Cup]]]] Sarajevo enjoyed a second successful period between 1978 and 1985, driven by the dynamic attacking duo of [[Predrag Pašić]] and Safet Sušić. This pair became one of the most prolific tandems in Yugoslav and Bosnian football history. Predrag Pašić, nicknamed "Paja," was a winger or striker who rose through the club's youth ranks and played for Sarajevo until his move to [[VfB Stuttgart]] after the title-winning season in 1985. Safet Sušić, known as "Pape," was a playmaker and attacking midfielder who donned the maroon and white jersey from 1973 until his transfer to [[Paris Saint-Germain F.C.|Paris Saint-Germain]] in 1982. In the 1978–79 season, Sušić scored 15 goals and was named Player of the Season as Sarajevo finished fourth. The following year, his 17 goals not only retained his Player of the Year title but also made him the joint-top scorer in the league. In the 1979–80 season, Sarajevo finished as runners-up, seven points behind Red Star Belgrade,{{cite news |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joeg80.html |title=SFR Yugoslavia First League 1979/80 |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation |date=25 July 2014 |access-date=3 February 2023 |archive-date=19 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230319161902/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joeg80.html |url-status=live }} therefore qualifying for the 1980–81 [[UEFA Cup]]. Sarajevo was knocked out in the first round by German powerhouse [[Hamburger SV]], which won 7–5 on aggregate.{{cite news |url=http://uk.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/season=1980/matches/round=1103/index.html |title=Sarajevo v Hamburg Sept/Oct 1980 |publisher=UEFA |date=25 July 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140202132917/http://uk.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/season%3D1980/matches/round%3D1103/index.html |archive-date=2 February 2014 }} Sarajevo returned to the UEFA Corvinul Hunedoara|Corvinul Hunedoara]] 8–4 in the second, thanks to a 4–0 home win in the second leg.{{cite news |url=http://uk.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/season=1982/matches/round=1116/index.html |title=Sarajevo v Corvinul Hunedoara Oct 1982 |publisher=UEFA |date=25 July 2014 |url-status=dead 16), Sarajevo lost the first leg 6–1 to Belgian club [[RSC Anderlecht]], and despite winning the second leg 1–0, were eliminated by the eventual champions.{{cite news |url=http://uk.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/season=1982/matches/round=1117/index.html |title=Sarajevo v Anderlecht Nov 1982 |publisher=UEFA |date=25 July 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921060917/http://uk.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/season%3D1982/matches/round%3D1117/index.html |archive-date=21 September 2013 }} Sarajevo also reached the Yugoslav Cup final that season, losing 3–2 to Dinamo Zagreb in Belgrade.{{cite news |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joegcupdetail.html |title=Cup of SFR Yugoslavia 1982/83 |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation |date=25 July 2014 |access-date=3 February 2023 |archive-date=9 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221209152002/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joegcupdetail.html |url-status=live }} Sarajevo secured their second championship title in the 1984–85 season, finishing four points ahead of runners-up Hajduk Split.{{cite news |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joeg85.html |title=SFR Yugoslavia First League 1984/85 |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation |date=25 July 2014 |access-date=3 February 2023 |archive-date=26 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221126120639/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joeg85.html |url-status=live }} The new championship season for Sarajevo didn't start spectacularly, but as it progressed, the team gained momentum and secured first place by the winter break.{{cite web|url=http://www.fksarajevo.ba/historija|title=FK Sarajevo historija|publisher=fksarajevo.ba|language=bs|trans-title=FK Sarajevo History|access-date=12 August 2014}}{{Dead link|date=March 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Boško Antić's team struggled at the beginning of the second half of the season, earning only two points from their first three matches. Their main rival, Hajduk Split, also had a slow start, winning just one of their first three games, which allowed Sarajevo to maintain a one-point lead. Antić's squad then defeated Sloboda and drew with Dinamo Zagreb and Željezničar before traveling to Split for a crucial match against Hajduk. A packed Poljud Stadium saw a 0–0 draw, preserving Sarajevo's narrow lead. The title race ultimately came down to Sarajevo and Hajduk Split, with both teams securing hard-fought victories. Three games before the season's end, Hajduk had a straightforward win over Rijeka, while Sarajevo faced a tough match in Novi Sad against Vojvodina. The hosts scored early, but Sarajevo equalized ten minutes before the break through a Jakovljević goal and eventually won seven minutes from time with a stunning volley from [[Slaviša Vukićević]]. Now needing just five points from their last three games to clinch the title, Sarajevo achieved a routine 3–0 victory over Iskra, followed by a challenging 2–2 draw against Vardar in [[Skopje]], after coming back from a 2–0 deficit just before halftime. Everything hinged on the final league game against Red Star Belgrade at a sold-out Koševo Stadium, where Sarajevo needed just a point to secure the title. [[Husref Musemić|Musemić]] opened the scoring in the 23rd minute, and [[Dragan Jakovljević|Jakovljević]] doubled the lead with fifteen minutes remaining. Although [[Boško Gjurovski]] pulled one back for the visitors in the 85th minute, it was too late to change the outcome. The celebrations began, Sarajevo had won its second Yugoslav league title.{{cite web |title=Jugoslavija |trans-title=Yugoslavia |website=Nogometni leksikon |language=hr |year=2008 |publisher=[[Miroslav Krleža Lexicographical Institute]] |url=http://nogomet.lzmk.hr/clanak.aspx?id=1004 |access-date=5 April 2014 |archive-date=7 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140407090456/http://nogomet.lzmk.hr/clanak.aspx?id=1004 |url-status=live }} The triumph qualified the club for the first round of the 1985–86 European Cup, where they shockingly lost both legs to Finnish side [[FC Kuusysi|Kuusysi Lahti]].{{cite news |url=http://uk.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/season=1985/matches/round=1044/index.html |title=Sarajevo v Lahti Sept 1985 |publisher=UEFA |date=25 July 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921060617/http://uk.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/season%3D1985/matches/round%3D1044/index.html |archive-date=21 September 2013 }} This result is still considered Sarajevo's worst in major European competitions. The championship winning generation included the likes of [[Husref Musemić]], [[Faruk Hadžibegić]], [[Davor Jozić]], [[Dragan Jakovljević]], [[Miloš Đurković]], [[Predrag Pašić]], [[Mirza Kapetanović]], [[Slaviša Vukićević]], [[Zijad Švrakić]], [[Senad Merdanović]] and [[Mehmed Janjoš]].{{cite web|url=https://www.worldfootball.net/teams/te793/fk-sarajevo/squad/|title=FK Sarajevo Squad 1984/1985|publisher=Worldfootball.net|access-date=20 August 2014|archive-date=21 August 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140821094223/http://www.worldfootball.net/teams/fk-sarajevo/1985/2/|url-status=live}} =====Final years in Yugoslavia===== FK Sarajevo entered a turbulent period after clinching its second Yugoslav league title. Three major members of the championship-winning squad left the team in the summer of 1985. Star striker Husref Musemić joined Red Star Belgrade. Faruk Hadžibegić moved to Spanish side [[Real Betis]]. Team captain Predrag Pašić moved to [[VfB Stuttgart]] in the [[Bundesliga]].{{cite web|url=http://fksinfo.com/bordo-vremeplov/bordo-vremeplov-ix-1985---1992/2227|title=Bordo vremeplov IX (1985–1992)|publisher=Fksinfo.com|language=bs|access-date=12 August 2014|archive-date=20 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140920221142/http://fksinfo.com/bordo-vremeplov/bordo-vremeplov-ix-1985---1992/2227|url-status=live}} The club management, in search of replacements, turned its sights to young players from lower-tier sides, bringing in [[Bernard Barnjak]], [[Vladimir Petković]] and Zoran Ljubičić. Even though the team started the season on a high note, it finished a disappointing 15th at the end of the 1985/86 season, avoiding relegation by virtue of a superior goal difference compared to relegated [[OFK Beograd]]. The following season again culminated in a lowly finish, as new manager [[Denijel Pirić]] led the team to a disappointing 13th place in the league standings. Further departures followed at the end of the season as [[Miloš Đurković]] joined [[Beşiktaş J.K.|Beşiktaş]], [[Muhidin Teskeredžić]] made the move to [[SK Sturm Graz|Sturm Graz]], [[Davor Jozić]] joined [[Serie A]] side [[A.C. Cesena|Cesena]], [[Zijad Švrakić]] transferred to [[Adana Demirspor]] and [[Branko Bošnjak (footballer)|Branko Bošnjak]] joined [[NK Olimpija Ljubljana (1945–2005)|Olimpija]]. The following two seasons again brought mediocre league finishes as the maroon-whites concluded the respective campaigns on 13th and 14th spots, barely avoiding relegation on both occasions. As with previous seasons, a handful of players left the club during the summer transfer window, with [[Slaviša Vukićević]] moving to [[US Créteil-Lusitanos|Créteil]], goalkeeper [[Enver Lugušić]] joining [[Konyaspor]] and [[Dragan Jakovljević]] moving to [[FC Nantes|Nantes]]. On a positive note, the [[1989–90 FK Sarajevo season|1989–90 season]] brought the return of fan-favorite Husref Musemić, who had spent the previous season playing for Scottish side [[Heart of Midlothian F.C.|Hearts]]. His nine goals in 26 appearances did little to improve league results, as the team again concluded the campaign in 13th spot, along with an early exit in the [[Yugoslav Cup]] after a defeat to Macedonian third division minnows, [[FK Sileks|Sileks]]. The [[1990-91 FK Sarajevo season|1990-91 season]] saw [[Fuad Muzurović]] again being named manager after a ten-year absence. Furthermore, [[Soviet]] goalkeeper [[Aleksei Prudnikov]] was brought in from [[FK Velež Mostar|Velež Mostar]], thus becoming the first foreign player in the history of the club. The team was able to conclude the season in 11th spot, defeating [[Red Star Belgrade]] in a crucial, hallmark game, only days after the Belgrade outfit won the [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]]. The [[1991-92 FK Sarajevo season|1991-92 season]] was marked by the disintegration of [[Yugoslavia]], and was subsequently abandoned by Slovenian, Croatian and Bosnian sides.{{cite web|url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joeg92.html|title=Yugoslavia 1991/92|publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation|access-date=12 August 2014|archive-date=9 July 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220709072103/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesj/joeg92.html|url-status=live}} Football was abruptly halted in Bosnia and Herzegovina for the duration of the war that would last for four years. Notable FK Sarajevo players in the pre-war period were [[Miloš Nedić]], [[Dragan Jakovljević]], [[Boban Božović]], [[Dane Kuprešanin]] and [[Dejan Raičković]]. ===Recent years=== Since the Bosnian independence, the club has won 14 domestic trophies, 5 of which were [[Premier League of Bosnia and Herzegovina]] honors. In addition the club reached play-off stage/final qualifying round for European competitions on 4 occasions, once for UCL (vs [[FC Dynamo Kyiv|Dynamo Kyiv]]) and three for UEL (vs [[CFR Cluj]], [[Borussia Mönchengladbach]] and [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]]). ====War and independence==== The [[Bosnian War]] in the early 1990s shut down competitive football in the territory, and as a result FK Sarajevo became a touring club in 1993, under manager [[Fuad Muzurović]], featuring players such as [[Elvir Baljić]], [[Almir Turković]], [[Senad Repuh]] and [[Mirza Varešanović]], all future national team players for [[Bosnia and Herzegovina national football team|Bosnia and Herzegovina]]. Many of the club's supporters, including the infamous [[Horde Zla]] joined the [[Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina]] and fought in the war. FK Sarajevo played a number of friendly games during this time, such as the now-famous 4–1 victory over the local UN peacekeeping force in 1994, a 1–1 draw against [[Parma F.C.]] while on tour in Italy, and a 3–1 victory over the [[Iran national football team|Iranian national team]] in Teheran. In 1994–95, the first-ever Bosnia and Herzegovina championship was held. Sarajevo came first in their six-team league in Jablanica, and came runners-up in the final league stage in [[Zenica]], behind local club [[NK Čelik Zenica|Čelik]].{{cite news |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesb/bih95.html |title=First Bosnian Championship 1994/95 |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation |date=25 July 2014 |access-date=3 February 2023 |archive-date=7 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221207235155/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesb/bih95.html |url-status=live }} Sarajevo again finished as runners-up to Čelik in 1996–97 (by two points),{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesb/bih97.html |title=Bosnia-Hercegovina 'Muslim' championship 1996/97 |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation |date=25 July 2014 |access-date=3 February 2023 |archive-date=24 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221024042356/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesb/bih97.html |url-status=live }} but beat the Zenica-based club in the Cup final and Super Cup. The Cup was retained the following year, and despite finishing third in the league, Sarajevo was runner-up due to play-offs. There was no play-off in 1998–99; the title was given to Sarajevo but it does not count.{{cite news |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesb/bihcup99.html |title=Bosnia-Hercegovina Federation Cup 1998/99 |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation |date=25 July 2014 |access-date=3 February 2023 |archive-date=3 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221203220913/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesb/bihcup99.html |url-status=live }} In 2004, [[Safet Sušić]], who played at FK Sarajevo from 1973 to 1982, was voted [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]]'s best player of the last 50 years at the [[UEFA Jubilee Awards]].{{cite news |url=https://www.rsssf.org/miscellaneous/uefa-awards.html |title=UEFA Awards: Bosnia's best player of the last 50 years: Safet Sušić |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation |date=25 July 2014 |access-date=3 February 2023 |archive-date=14 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220814123143/https://www.rsssf.org/miscellaneous/uefa-awards.html |url-status=live }} Sarajevo were runners-up in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Premier League in 2006–07, but won their second title the following season, beating [[Zrinjski Mostar]] by three points.{{cite news |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesb/bih07.html |title=Bosnia-Hercegovina Premijer Liga 2006/07 |publisher=Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation |date=25 July 2014 |access-date=3 February 2023 |archive-date=24 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221024042356/https://www.rsssf.org/tablesb/bih07.html |url-status=live }} Sarajevo have been a regular in [[Europa League]] qualification in the 21st century, but are yet to make the group stages. Off the back of their [[2006–07 Premier League of Bosnia and Herzegovina|2006–07 league title]] under manager Husref Musemić, Sarajevo played in the [[UEFA Champions League]] for the first time in its current format. They beat Maltese champions [[Marsaxlokk F.C.]] 6:0 away in their first game, eventually winning 9:1 on aggregate.{{cite news |url=http://uk.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/season=2008/matches/round=15102/index.html |title=Sarajevo v Marsaxlokk July 2007 |publisher=UEFA |date=25 July 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222152032/http://uk.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/season%3D2008/matches/round%3D15102/index.html |archive-date=22 February 2014 }} The second round saw Sarajevo defeat Belgians [[KRC Genk]] on away goals due to a 2:1 away win in the first leg,{{cite news |url=http://uk.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/season=2008/matches/round=15103/index.html |title=Sarajevo v Genk July 2007 |publisher=UEFA |date=25 July 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222152030/http://uk.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/season%3D2008/matches/round%3D15103/index.html |archive-date=22 February 2014 }} although the club was knocked out in the play-offs for the competition's Group stage by Ukrainian champions [[Dynamo Kyiv]] who won 4:0 on aggregate.{{cite news |url=http://uk.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/season=2008/matches/round=15104/index.html |title=Sarajevo v Dynamo Kyiv Aug 2007 |publisher=UEFA |date=25 July 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222151938/http://uk.uefa.com/uefachampionsleague/season%3D2008/matches/round%3D15104/index.html |archive-date=22 February 2014 }} The club made the play-offs round of the [[2009–10 UEFA Europa League]] and faced [[CFR Cluj]] but lost 3–2 on aggregate. The team defeated [[FC Spartak Trnava|Spartak Trnava]] and [[Helsingborgs IF|Helsingborg]] to get to the playoff round. ====Vincent Tan era: A financial injection==== [[File:Vincent Tan Chee Yioun.jpg|thumb|left|upright|[[Vincent Tan]] was worth an estimated US$1.6 [[1,000,000,000 (number)|billion]] in 2014{{cite web|title=#1122 Vincent Tan|url=https://www.forbes.com/profile/vincent-tan/|work=[[Forbes]]|access-date=28 April 2014|archive-date=22 March 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190322094622/https://www.forbes.com/profile/vincent-tan/|url-status=live}}]] [[Vincent Tan]], a [[Malaysians|Malaysian]] businessman and the owner of the [[Football League Championship|Championship]] club [[Cardiff City F.C.|Cardiff City]], bought FK Sarajevo in late 2013 pledging to invest $2 million into the club.{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2013/dec/25/cardiff-city-vincent-tan-bosnia |title=Cardiff City owner Vincent Tan takes control of club in Bosnia |newspaper=The Guardian |date=25 December 2013 |access-date=11 December 2016 |archive-date=11 February 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170211082001/https://www.theguardian.com/football/2013/dec/25/cardiff-city-vincent-tan-bosnia |url-status=live }} Under the deal, Cardiff will cooperate with FK Sarajevo, exchanging players and taking part in a football academy, yet to be established, which Tan has said would lure new talents. Under Tan's management the club brought in quality players with the likes of [[Miloš Stojčev]], [[Džemal Berberović]] and [[Nemanja Bilbija]] who helped the club win the [[2013–14 Bosnia and Herzegovina Football Cup|2013–14]] Bosnian Cup, their first silverware since winning the Premier League in 2006–07.{{cite web|url=http://balkans.aljazeera.net/vijesti/nogometasi-sarajeva-osvojili-kup-bih|title=Nogometaši Sarajeva osvojili Kup BiH|trans-title=FK Sarajevo won the Bosnian Cup|language=bs|publisher=Al Jazeera|access-date=17 March 2014|archive-date=26 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140526015331/http://balkans.aljazeera.net/vijesti/nogometasi-sarajeva-osvojili-kup-bih|url-status=live}} Prior to the Cup triumph, [[Robert Jarni]] was brought in as the new manager of the club in December 2013 by Tan, but was quickly dismissed only 4 months into his tenure (on 7 April 2014, while the team was still in the semi-finals of the Bosnian Cup) due to the team failing to keep its chances of winning the domestic league title alive during later stages of the 2013–14 season.{{cite web|url=http://www.walesonline.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/vincent-tan-sacks-manager-fk-6934647|title=Vincent Tan sacks manager: FK Sarajevo boss Robert Jarni axed|publisher=Wales Online|access-date=17 March 2014|archive-date=10 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140410165400/http://www.walesonline.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/vincent-tan-sacks-manager-fk-6934647|url-status=live}} FK Sarajevo played a friendly match against Tan's [[Cardiff City F.C. Under-23s and Academy|Cardiff City U21]] winning 4–1.{{cite news|url=http://www.radiosarajevo.ba/novost/158472/foto-uspjesna-generalka-bordo-tima-sarajevo-bolje-od-juniora-cardiffa|title=Sarajevo 4 – 1 Cardiff City U21s|date=23 March 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714124422/http://www.radiosarajevo.ba/novost/158472/foto-uspjesna-generalka-bordo-tima-sarajevo-bolje-od-juniora-cardiffa|archive-date=14 July 2014}} In 2014–15 UEFA Europa League, FK Sarajevo eliminated [[FK Haugesund]] and [[Atromitos F.C.|Atromitos]] to qualify for the [[2014–15 UEFA Europa League qualifying phase and play-off round#Play-off round|play-off round]], where it lost to German side [[Borussia Mönchengladbach]]. The club’s traditional home kit typically consists of a maroon jersey, paired with white shorts and maroon socks. Originally, the club colours were [[sky blue]] and white.{{cite web|url=https://www.bordovremeplov.ba/Igrac/Details?id=1722|title=Lav Mantula|website=bordovremeplov.ba|accessdate=2023-07-03}} The change came about in the summer of 1962 when Sarajevo was drawn with [[Servette FC]] in the Rapan Cup, whose captain was former Sarajevo player [[Lav Mantula]]. After their fixture in Sarajevo, Mantula visited the club offices, and in a conversation with the management, suggested that Sarajevo adopt Servette's club colours because no team in Yugoslavia at the time had maroon as its main colour. The idea was accepted at the next club assembly, officially establishing maroon as the club’s defining colour.{{cite web|url=https://www.klix.ba/sport/nogomet/znate-li-koje-su-bile-prve-boje-fk-sarajevo/170522035|title=Znate li koje su bile prve boje FK Sarajevo?|date=22 May 2017|access-date=19 December 2023|language=bs|author=|publisher=Klix.ba}} Maroon has since become deeply embedded in the club’s visual identity and is widely recognized throughout Sarajevo and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The club also uses deep maroon (Pantone 4625 C / #5D0D10) and white (Pantone 7436 C / #FFFFFF) in its branding.{{cite web|url=https://fk-sarajevo.ba/bs/klub/grb-i-boje/2|title=Grb i boje|date=15 June 2025|access-date=15 June 2025|language=bs|author=|publisher=fk-sarajevo.ba}} The first official club crest featured a [[red star]], a [[Five-pointed star|five-pointed]] [[symbol]] that has historically been associated with [[Communism|communist ideology]] and was commonly used across post-WWII Yugoslavia. In 1949, the crest was modified to feature golden borders enclosing a golden silhouette of a footballer. Additionally, a blue industrial gear within a circular frame, symbolizing socialist industrialization, included the club's name.{{cite web|url=http://www.weltfussballarchiv.com/club-profile/bosnia-and-herzegovina/fk-sarajevo/14048/|title=FK Sarajevo crest history|publisher=Weltfussballarchiv.com|access-date=20 August 2014|archive-date=29 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141029001542/http://www.weltfussballarchiv.com/club-profile/bosnia-and-herzegovina/fk-sarajevo/14048/|url-status=live}} In 1962, the club crest was changed for the third time. It adopted a badge-like shape, divided vertically into two sections: the outer section displayed the club's name and the communist star, while the inner section featured a football and the club's founding year. After the [[Bosnian War]] ended in 1996, the crest was slightly modified. The communist star was replaced with a [[Lilium bosniacum|Bosnian fleur-de-lis]], and the design, including the lettering font, was slightly stylized. This updated crest became one of the club's most recognizable trademarks in the following years. The adding of fleur-de-lis motifs to their crests was a common practice by Bosnian football clubs in the first few years after the war. The fleur-de-lis was eventually removed from the club crest in 2007, which today lacks any ideological or national symbols.{{cite web|url=http://www.fksarajevo.ba/grb|title=FK Sarajevo Crest|publisher=Fksarajevo.ba|access-date=20 August 2014}}{{Dead link|date=March 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Despite this, the club continues to embrace its visual heritage. [[Yugoslavia|Yugoslav]]-era crests are frequently featured on official merchandise and retro collections.{{cite web|url=https://fk-sarajevo.ba/bs/clanak/pogledajte-novu-retro-kolekciju-iz-fk-sarajevo-shopa/6762|title=Pogledajte novu retro kolekciju iz FK Sarajevo shopa|date=8 September 2022|access-date=19 December 2023|language=bs|author=|publisher=fk-sarajevo.ba}} The fleur-de-lis made a brief return in the [[2013–14 FK Sarajevo season|2013–14 season]] as part of the club’s third kit.{{cite web|url=https://fk-sarajevo.ba/bs/clanak/predstavljen-treci-dres-fk-sarajevo-za-sezonu-2013-2014/450|title=Predstavljen treći dres FK Sarajevo za sezonu 2013/2014|date=15 July 2013|access-date=19 December 2023|language=bs|author=|publisher=fk-sarajevo.ba}} {| style="width:100%; color:#5d0d10;" | 2001–2007 | style="font-weight:600; color:#5d0d10;" | 2007–present |} ==Stadium and training grounds== {{Main|Koševo City Stadium|Butmir Training Centre}} [[File:Asim Ferhatović Hase Stadium.jpg|thumb|[[Koševo City Stadium]], also known as the Asim Ferhatović - Hase Stadium]] FK Sarajevo plays at the [[Asim Ferhatović Hase Stadium]], formerly known as the Koševo Stadium. It is owned by the City of Sarajevo but is leased to the club on a long-term basis. The club runs and operates the stadium and has sole commercial and developmental rights to the Olympic complex until at least 2051, with the possibility of a further 15-year extension.{{cite web|url=https://reprezentacija.ba/324429-nacelnik-srdan-mandic-svecano-urucio-stadion-asim-ferhatovic-hase-fk-sarajevo|title=Načelnik Srđan Mandić svečano uručio stadion "Asim Ferhatović Hase" FK Sarajevo|publisher=Reprezentacija.ba|access-date=2 May 2021|archive-date=2 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210502004458/https://reprezentacija.ba/324429-nacelnik-srdan-mandic-svecano-urucio-stadion-asim-ferhatovic-hase-fk-sarajevo|url-status=live}} The current seating capacity is 34,700. The stadium was opened in 1947 and named after the Sarajevo neighborhood of '''Koševo''', where it is located.{{cite web|url=http://www.footballgroundmap.com/ground/asim-ferhatovic-hase-stadium/fk-sarajevo/bosnia-and-herzegovina|title=Asim Ferhatović Hase Stadium|publisher=Footballgroundmap.com|access-date=20 August 2014|archive-date=21 August 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140821125924/http://www.footballgroundmap.com/ground/asim-ferhatovic-hase-stadium/fk-sarajevo/bosnia-and-herzegovina|url-status=live}} The stadium was literally buried into a local hill thus merging with its natural surroundings. In 1950 a pitch and a tartan track were also added. The first international football match at the stadium was played between [[Yugoslavia national football team|Yugoslavia]] and [[Turkey national football team|Turkey]], in 1954. In 1966, the stadium hosted the [[Balkan Games]] and was again renovated for the occasion.{{cite web|url=http://www.gbrathletics.com/ic/bg.htm|title=Balkan Games stats|publisher=Gbrathletics.com|access-date=20 August 2014|archive-date=26 January 2002|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020126101538/http://www.gbrathletics.com/ic/bg.htm|url-status=live}} A new administration building was built, as were new locker rooms and a restaurant. A modern scoreboard and new lighting were also provided. In 1984, the stadium was reconstructed for the [[1984 Winter Olympics]] that were held in Sarajevo and is therefore often unofficially called ''The Olympic Stadium''.{{cite web|url=http://www.thewire.com/global/2014/02/scenes-sarajevo-olympics-and-after-war/357793/|title=Scenes from Sarajevo: From the Olympics to War and Back Again|work=The Wire|access-date=20 August 2014|archive-date=21 August 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140821181839/http://www.thewire.com/global/2014/02/scenes-sarajevo-olympics-and-after-war/357793/|url-status=live}} On 7 February 1984, the Asim H. Ferhatović stadium hosted the opening ceremony of the games, and seated roughly 50,000. The West stand held 18,500 seating places at the time.[http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/1984/or1984w.pdf 1984 Winter Olympics official report.] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111126020725/http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/1984/or1984w.pdf |date=26 November 2011 }} pp. 10–14, 90. In 2004 the stadium's official name was changed to '''Asim H. Ferhatović''', in memory of legendary FK Sarajevo striker [[Asim Ferhatović]], who died after a heart attack in 1987.{{cite web|url=http://www.vesti.rs/Feljton/Sarajevski-smeker-u-kopackama-Asim-Ferhatovic-Hase-3.html|title=Sarajevski šmeker u kopačkama: Asim Ferhatović Hase|publisher=Vesti.rs|access-date=20 August 2014|archive-date=29 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141029001641/http://www.vesti.rs/Feljton/Sarajevski-smeker-u-kopackama-Asim-Ferhatovic-Hase-3.html|url-status=live}} In 1998, three years after the end of the [[Bosnian War]], the stadium was renovated for a fourth time. The seating capacity of the stadium was reduced to 34,500 and new seats were added.{{cite web|url=http://stadiumdb.com/stadiums/bih/olimpijskij_stadion_kosevo|title=Asim Ferhatović Hase Stadium|publisher=StadiumDB.com|access-date=20 August 2014|archive-date=14 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170214100820/http://stadiumdb.com/stadiums/bih/olimpijskij_stadion_kosevo|url-status=live}} The ground has held matches for Sarajevo and their local rival Željezničar, including Europa League and Champions League fixtures. Furthermore, the stadium has hosted the national teams of [[Yugoslavia national football team|Yugoslavia]] and [[Bosnia and Herzegovina national football team|Bosnia and Herzegovina]] on numerous occasions, as well as many notable athletic meetings. Throughout its football history, the stadium welcomed some of Europe's finest clubs such as [[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]], [[Real Madrid CF|Real Madrid]], [[Derby County F.C.|Derby County]], [[Inter Milan]], [[Hamburger SV]], [[Newcastle United F.C.|Newcastle United]], [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]], [[Anderlecht]], [[Borussia Mönchengladbach]], [[FC Dynamo Kyiv|Dynamo Kyiv]], [[FC Basel|Basel]], and others. Notable non-European clubs that have played Sarajevo on the stadium include the likes of [[Santos FC|Santos]] and [[SE Palmeiras| Palmeiras]]. The stadium's highest attendance was recorded in a 1981–82 league match between FK Sarajevo and their city rival [[FK Željezničar Sarajevo|FK Željezničar]]. Allegedly, roughly 60,000 people attended the game. [[File:Butmir training center.jpg|thumb|[[Butmir Training Centre]]]] The club’s current training facility, the [[Butmir Training Centre]], is located in the municipality of [[Ilidža]], within the Sarajevo Canton. The complex was officially opened in October 2015 and covers an area of approximately 70,000 square meters (17 acres).{{cite web|url=https://fk-sarajevo.ba/vijesti/otvoren-trening-centar-u-butmiru/2367|title=Otvoren Trening Centar u Butmiru|date=24 October 2015|access-date=16 June 2025|language=bs|publisher=FK Sarajevo}} facilities, player accommodation, a clinic, and administrative offices.{{cite web|url=https://sport.avaz.ba/nogomet/148701/fk-sarajevo-novi-trening-centar-u-butmiru-bit-ce-najmoderniji-u-bih|title=FK Sarajevo: Novi trening centar u Butmiru biće najmoderniji u BiH|date=18 May 2015|access-date=16 June 2025|language=bs|publisher=Dnevni Avaz}} It serves as the primary training ground for the club’s first team, as well as for its youth academy, B team and women’s team.{{cite web|url=https://fk-sarajevo.ba/vijesti/zfk-sarajevo-pocinje-pripreme-u-butmiru/2962|title=ŽFK Sarajevo počinje pripreme u guarantee]] and [[corporate personhood]] that, unlike football clubs that are registered as [[limited companies]], does not [[Issued shares|issue shares]] by which individuals or corporations can buy majority or minority ownership. Instead, the club's members act as guarantors by buying non-ownership-based management stakes in the form of contributions, earning in return management and voting rights.{{cite web|url=http://mks.ks.gov.ba/sites/mks.ks.gov.ba/files/zakonsport.pdf|title=Zakon o sportu Kantona Sarajevo|publisher=Službene novine Kantona Sarajevo|access-date=3 August 2016|archive-date=13 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150413135700/http://mks.ks.gov.ba/sites/mks.ks.gov.ba/files/ZakonSport.pdf|url-status=live}} The guarantors give an undertaking to contribute a nominal amount in the event of the winding up of the company. It is often believed that such a company cannot distribute its profits to its members but, depending on the provisions of the articles, as is the case with FK Sarajevo, it very well may.{{cite book|author=Hannigan, B.|title=Company Law|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2003|isbn=978-0-406-91356-2}} Managing rights imply the right to form and control the club assembly, steering committee, and supervisory board, by which the largest contributor ''de iure'' takes full control of the club.{{cite web|url=http://balkans.aljazeera.net/vijesti/vincent-tan-vecinski-vlasnik-fk-sarajevo|title=Vincent Tan većinski vlasnik FK Sarajevo|publisher=Al Jazeera|access-date=3 August 2016|archive-date=28 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160828034936/http://balkans.aljazeera.net/vijesti/vincent-tan-vecinski-vlasnik-fk-sarajevo|url-status=live}} Furthermore, the fact that the largest contributor may negotiate profit provisions between himself and the club opens the possibility for large-scale financial investment that exceeds charitable and non-profit contributions that are usually the cornerstone of companies limited by guarantee. Malaysian billionaire, investor, and former chairman of [[Berjaya Group]], [[Vincent Tan]], was the club's majority contributor and thus its sole operator. After gaining control of the club in December 2013 by contributing US$2 million, Tan negotiated an agreement between himself and the club, by which he will invest an undisclosed sum while also running the operational finances and policies of the club, in return gaining the right to profit as would be the case of the club being a limited company. Furthermore, the formation of [[Public limited company|Public limited companies]] in the fields of real estate and tourism has been negotiated between the club and Tan, by which the companies will represent a joint venture by both parties, earning the club complete financial self-sustainability in the future. After taking control of the club, Vincent Tan dissolved the long-standing steering committee and supervisory board, opting to create a five-member board of directors for the day-to-day running of the club. 23 May 2022 – 23 November 2022 |- | [[Senijad Ibričić]] | 3 August 2023 – 3 June 2024 |} ===Memorials=== {{Collapse top|title=Memorials established by the club|collapsed=yes}} [[File:Spomen ploča ARBiH.jpg|thumb|Memorial on the north side of the [[Koševo City Stadium|Koševo Stadium]]]] * '''[[Horde zla]]''' : The club raised a memorial outside of the north stand of the Asim Ferhatović Hase Stadium which bears tribute to hundreds of members of the club's [[ultras]] group, Horde zla, killed in the defense of the city during the [[Siege of Sarajevo]]. * '''[[Svetozar Vujović]]''' : Svetozar Vujović played for the club from 1959 to 1972, serving as a key figure in the 1967 championship-winning team. After his playing career, he briefly managed the club for one season before assuming the role of club director, a position he held for more than two decades. When the Siege of Sarajevo began in 1992, Vujović chose to remain in the city, turning down numerous offers of refuge. After his passing on January 16, 1993, FK Sarajevo honored him by naming the club’s main ceremonial lounge in its downtown administrative facility "The Svetozar Vujović Salon."{{Cite web |work=Avaz |title=Novi pres salon: Svetozar Vujović, čovjek čije je ime kucalo za FK Sarajevo |date=23 February 2018 |url=https://avaz.ba/domaci-nogomet/354693/novi-pres-salon-svetozar-vujovic-covjek-cije-je-ime-kucalo-za-fk-sarajevo |access-date=11 May 2025}} * '''[[Asim Ferhatović]]''' : Asim Ferhatović, a legendary forward for the club, scored 66 goals in 174 league appearances, making him the club’s all-time leading scorer in official competitions. Widely regarded as one of the greatest players to don the maroon-white jersey, Ferhatović’s legacy lives on through the Koševo Stadium, which bears his name following his death in 1987. Additionally, the club’s School of Football, a key part of its youth program, is named in his honor. * '''[[Želimir Vidović]]''' : Želimir Vidović was a standout player for the club in the 1970s and early 1980s. On May 17, 1992, during the Siege of Sarajevo, Vidović participated in an operation to transport wounded civilians to a hospital in the [[Dobrinja]] neighborhood. The convoy was intercepted by Serb forces, and Vidović was executed, with his remains later discovered in a mass grave. Since 2004, an annual tournament has been held in his honor, and the main pitch at the [[Butmir Training Centre]] is named after him. A statue of Vidović stands on the western grass knoll surrounding the field.{{Cite web |work=N1 BiH |date=17 May 2024 |title=Prije 32 godine ubijen je heroj u kopačkama Želimir Vidović Keli |url=https://n1info.ba/sport/nogomet/prije-32-godine-ubijen-je-heroj-u-kopackama-zelimir-vidovic-keli/ |access-date=2025-05-11}} * '''[[#Ismir Pintol trophy|Ismir Pintol]]''' : Ismir Pintol, a 6-year-old FK Sarajevo supporter, died on June 29, 2002, after a long battle with leukemia. In his memory, the club, in partnership with Horde zla, established the [[#Ismir Pintol trophy|Ismir Pintol trophy]] ("Trofej Ismir Pintol"), awarded to the standout player of the previous season. This tradition began in the 2002–03 season. To honor Ismir, fans remain seated in silence for the first six minutes of the final home game each season. The trophy is presented before kick-off at the base of the north stand.{{Cite web |work=Klix |date=20 May 2024 |title=Horde zla izabrale dobitnika nagrade: Ismir Pintol za kratko vrijeme postao je miljenik navijača |url=https://www.klix.ba/sport/nogomet/horde-zla-izabrale-dobitnika-nagrade-ismir-pintol-za-kratko-vrijeme-postao-je-miljenik-navijaca/240520050 |access-date=11 May 2025}} * '''[[2009 NK Široki Brijeg–FK Sarajevo football riots|Vedran Puljić]]''' : Vedran Puljić, a 24-year-old member of FK Sarajevo’s ultras group, Horde zla, was tragically killed by a single gunshot during the notorious [[2009 NK Široki Brijeg–FK Sarajevo football riots|Široki Brijeg football riots]] on October 4, 2009. The team has been affiliated with the men's team since 2015, following a merger agreement signed on July 4, after which the club adopted the FK Sarajevo crest and colors.{{cite web|title=Zvanično: Nogometašice SFK 2000 postale dio Bordo porodice|url=http://sport033.com/zvanicno-nogometasice-sfk-2000-postale-dio-bordo-porodice/|website=sport033.com|access-date=4 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150705105128/http://sport033.com/zvanicno-nogometasice-sfk-2000-postale-dio-bordo-porodice/|archive-date=5 July 2015|url-status=dead}} The club was established in June 2000 as part of the ''Alija Miladin'' recreational society, subsequently affiliating with a now-defunct men's football team from Sarajevo's Otoka neighborhood. They play their home games in the domestic league at the [[Butmir Training Centre]] and European fixtures at [[Koševo Stadium]]. Since its inception, the club has become the dominant force in Bosnian women's football, securing 23 consecutive national titles, 22 consecutive national cups (22 doubles), and representing the country in European competitions. It is also the most decorated women's club in the former Yugoslavia.{{cite web|title=Nogometašice SFK 2000 potvrdile dominaciju u BiH|url=http://sport033.com/nogometasice-sfk-2000-potvrdile-dominaciju-u-bih/|website=sport033.com|access-date=4 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150705104100/http://sport033.com/nogometasice-sfk-2000-potvrdile-dominaciju-u-bih/|archive-date=5 July 2015|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|title=SFK 2000 historija|url=http://www.fksarajevo.ba/bs/sfk-2000|publisher=Official website|access-date=4 July 2015|archive-date=20 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160120235057/http://www.fksarajevo.ba/bs/sfk-2000|url-status=live}} The club has participated in the [[UEFA Women's Cup]] from 2003 onwards but never reached the final rounds. In the [[2009–10 UEFA Women's Champions League]], when the competition was rebranded and reorganized, the side reached the round of 32, a feat repeated during the [[2012–13 UEFA Women's Champions League|2012–13]] season. The side's best [[UEFA]] women's club ranking was 17th in August 2013. SFK 2000 players form the core of the [[Bosnia and Herzegovina women's national football team|Bosnia and Herzegovina women's national team]], while the club's current managing director [[Samira Hurem]], was the longstanding Bosnia & Herzegovina manager until 2024. On 29 August 2016 the club qualified for the Round of 32 in the Women's Champions League for a third time in its History.{{cite web|title=Nogometašice SFK Sarajevo remijem sa Kharkivom izborile plasman među 32 najbolje ekipe Evrope|url=http://www.klix.ba/sport/nogomet/nogometasice-sfk-sarajevo-remijem-sa-kharkivom-izborile-plasman-medju-32-najbolje-ekipe-evrope/160828063|publisher=Klix.ba|access-date=29 August 2016|archive-date=30 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160830031652/http://www.klix.ba/sport/nogomet/nogometasice-sfk-sarajevo-remijem-sa-kharkivom-izborile-plasman-medju-32-najbolje-ekipe-evrope/160828063|url-status=live}} On 1 September 2016 the team drew [[WFC Rossiyanka]] of Russia in the round of 32.{{cite web|title=SFK Sarajevo protiv Rossiyanke u šesnaestini finala Lige prvaka|url=http://www.klix.ba/sport/nogomet/sfk-sarajevo-protiv-rossiyanke-u-sesnaestini-finala-lige-prvaka/160901075|publisher=Klix.ba|access-date=2 September 2016|archive-date=5 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160905123426/http://www.klix.ba/sport/nogomet/sfk-sarajevo-protiv-rossiyanke-u-sesnaestini-finala-lige-prvaka/160901075|url-status=live}} The club once again qualified for the [[2018–19 UEFA Women's Champions League#Round of 32|round of 32]], this time in the [[2018–19 UEFA Women's Champions League]] season, but got eliminated by [[Chelsea F.C. In total, they’ve reached the Round of 32 four times, notably in 2009–10, 2012–13, 2018–19, and most recently on 4 September 2024, when they dominated [[KÍ Klaksvík]] 3–0 in the Round 1 mini‐tournament in Sarajevo. In the subsequent fixture on 7 September 2024, they faced [[S.L. Benfica (women)|SL Benfica]] and were defeated 4–0. Beyond their domestic and European success, SFK 2000 Sarajevo has garnered widespread recognition for its commitment to youth development and gender equality in sports. The club operates a comprehensive academy system that nurtures girls from an early age, providing them with professional coaching, access to elite facilities, and structured competition. Many of Bosnia's and Herzegovina’s top female footballers have risen through SFK’s ranks. The club also engages in outreach initiatives, often in collaboration with NGOs and international partners, promoting female participation in sport, especially in underserved communities.{{cite web | url=https://www.ecaeurope.com/news-media-releases/eca-youth-knowledge-exchange-pivotal-at-inaugural-wings-cup/ | title=ECA Youth Knowledge Exchange Pivotal at Inaugural Wings Cup | work=European Club Association | date=29 April 2025 | access-date=15 June 2025 | language=en | publisher=European Club Association}} As such, SFK 2000 is not only the sporting pride of Sarajevo but also a symbol of resilience, inclusion, and empowerment.{{cite web | url=https://www.klix.ba/sport/nogomet/akademija-sfk-2000-prvi-put-predstavljena-na-ino-sceni-eca-youth-football-exchange-dogadjaj-u-znaku-bh-prvakinja/240913083 | title=SFK 2000 Sarajevo istaknuo napore u razvoju ženskog nogometa na ECA Youth Football Exchange | date=13 September 2024 | access-date=15 June 2025 | language=bs | publisher=Klix.ba}} SFK 2000 operates a youth academy for girls from the ages of five to sixteen.{{cite web|title=SFK 2000 omladinski pogon|url=http://www.fksarajevo.ba/bs/sfk-2000|publisher=Official website|access-date=4 July 2016|archive-date=21 July 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160721212452/http://www.fksarajevo.ba/bs/sfk-2000|url-status=live}} The academy is one of the most renowned and export-oriented in Europe.{{cite web|title=The biggest Transfer in the History of Bosnian Women's Football!|url=https://sarajevotimes.com/the-biggest-transfer-in-the-history-of-bosnian-womens-football/|publisher=Sarajevo Times|access-date=4 July 2016}} Notable alumni include [[Inter Milan (women)|Inter Milan]] defender, [[Marija Milinković]]; [[Juventus FC (women)|Juventus]] defender, [[Gloria Slišković]]; [[Inter Milan (women)|Inter Milan]] forward, [[Maja Jelčić]]; [[AC Milan Women|Milan]] forward, [[Lidija Kuliš]] and [[Sporting CP (women's football)|Sporting]] defender, [[Melisa Hasanbegović]]. As of 17 December 2024, SFK 2000 is ranked 30th in Europe.{{cite web|url=https://www.eurotopteam.com/football/classfemme.php|title= Football Féminin - Classement des clubs|date=17 December 2023|access-date=19 December 2023|language=bs|author=|publisher=eurotopteam.com}} ==Supporters== {{Main|Horde Zla|Maroon Friends 1946}} [[File:Horde zla 2023.jpg|thumb|[[Horde Zla]] on the north stand of the Koševo Stadium, 8 October 2023]] FK Sarajevo is one of the two most popular clubs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, boasting a large fanbase across the country, the [[Sandžak]] region of [[Serbia]] and [[Montenegro]], and the [[Bosnian diaspora]]. This diaspora is especially prominent in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Scandinavia, Canada, Australia, and the United States. The largest diaspora fan association is registered in Stuttgart, Germany.{{cite web|url=https://www.klix.ba/sport/nogomet/i-st-louis-ima-svoj-fk-sarajevo-osnovan-fc-bordo/131121082|title=I St. Louis ima svoj FK Sarajevo: Osnovan FC Bordo|language=bs|publisher=Klix.ba|access-date=6 January 2023|archive-date=6 January 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230106224252/https://www.klix.ba/sport/nogomet/i-st-louis-ima-svoj-fk-sarajevo-osnovan-fc-bordo/131121082|url-status=live}} From its establishment on 24 October 1946, FK Sarajevo quickly garnered a following in the city of Sarajevo. The banning of nearly all pre-war Sarajevan clubs by the new communist authorities left a significant vacuum in a city traditionally known as a footballing center in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. The majority of fans came from the downtown neighborhoods of [[Baščaršija]], [[Stari Grad, Sarajevo|Stari grad]], and [[Centar Municipality, Sarajevo|Centar]], predominantly inhabited by [[Bosniaks]]. While other ethnicities supported the club in equal numbers, the history of organized support is nonetheless closely tied to these neighborhoods. FK Sarajevo fans have been historically called Pitari while an individual was, and is still known as a Pitar. The nickname, meaning a consumer of the local Bosnian dish ''[[Burek|pita]]'', was originally a derogatory label given by fans of working-class Željezničar that implied the pre-World War Two upper-class background of most FK Sarajevo supporters.{{cite web|url=http://www.hordezla.ba/index.php/o-nama|title=O nama|language=bs|publisher=Hordezla.ba|access-date=17 March 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140426221053/http://www.hordezla.ba/index.php/o-nama|archive-date=26 April 2014}} This stemmed from the fact that the old downtown neighborhoods of the city were traditional centers of commerce and artisanship, even though the socioeconomic landscape had dramatically changed by the time the club was founded. The organized supporters' group of Sarajevo, known as [[Horde zla]] ([[English language|English]]: Hordes of Evil or Gang Evil), was formed in 1987 with the arrival of the [[Ultras]] subculture to Yugoslavia. The group is located on the north stand of the Asim Ferhatović Hase Stadium and has a decentralized organizational structure with many subgroups present at matches. The group's name was borrowed from a [[Zagor (comics)|Zagor]] comic book at the time of its inception. Its logo features a stylized depiction of the [[Personifications of death|Grim Reaper]].
